summary: Specifies the U.S. Department of Defense Basic Security Option, and a top-level description of the Extended Security Option, for the Internet Protocol. These let packets carry security labels. It obsoletes RFC 1038. It is historic.

eli5.summary: Some packets are secret and some are not. This adds a label to each packet so the network knows how carefully to handle it.

questions: what is the ip basic security option
what are dod security labels in ip
what is the extended security option
subtitle: Two IP header options that stamp each packet with a U.S. security classification and who protects it.

tldr.problem: U.S. Department of Defense networks needed packets to carry security labels so end systems and gateways could check that each datagram may travel where it is going.
tldr.mechanism: The Basic Security Option (type 130) carries a classification level and protection authority flags. The Extended Security Option (type 133) carries extra label data whose format is set by separate RFCs.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1108 obsoletes RFC 1038 and is marked Historic.

today: RFC 1108 is marked Historic. It obsoletes RFC 1038, and no later RFC is recorded as replacing it.

sections.title: The Two DoD Security Options
sections.content:
RFC 1108 defines two IP options for U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) common user data networks. Both have class 0, are copied on fragmentation, and have variable length. DoD Basic Security is option number 2 (type 130) and carries the classification level and protection authority flags. DoD Extended Security is option number 5 (type 133) and carries additional security information required by registered authorities.

End systems and intermediate systems use the Basic option to carry common security labels from source to destination, to check that a datagram is appropriate to send and deliver, and to make sure the route is protected to the level every listed authority requires. For that last goal the RFC says interior and exterior gateway protocols must be augmented with security label information.
sections.eli5: There are two kinds of stickers. The basic one says how secret the packet is and whose rules apply. The extended one holds extra details for special cases.

sections.title: Format of the Basic Security Option
sections.content:
The option holds a Type of 130, a Length, a one-octet Classification Level, and a variable-length Protection Authority field. The minimum length is 3 octets, because the authority field may be absent. The option must be copied on fragmentation and appears at most once per datagram.

The classification values were chosen to keep a Hamming distance of four between any two valid values. Because the encodings are sparse, equality may be tested by comparing bit strings, but ordered range checks must not be done with plain arithmetic. Reserved values are invalid.

The authority field is a run of octets. The first seven bits of each octet are flags, one per authority, and the low-order bit is 1 if more octets follow and 0 for the last. Only one octet is needed at first, but a minimally compliant implementation must handle at least 2 octets, which is up to 14 authorities. No unassigned flag is valid, and no ordering is defined between two flag fields.
sections.eli5: The sticker has a secrecy level, such as Secret or Top Secret, plus little checkboxes for which agencies' rules apply.

sections.title: Security Configuration Parameters
sections.content:
A system that uses the option must be configured with protected parameters. System-wide settings are SYSTEM-LEVEL-MAX, SYSTEM-LEVEL-MIN, SYSTEM-AUTHORITY-IN and SYSTEM-AUTHORITY-OUT. Each network port has its own PORT-LEVEL-MAX, PORT-LEVEL-MIN, PORT-AUTHORITY-IN and PORT-AUTHORITY-OUT, plus PORT-AUTHORITY-ERROR, PORT-IMPLICIT-LABEL, PORT-BSO-REQUIRED-RECEIVE and PORT-BSO-REQUIRED-TRANSMIT.

The port ranges must sit inside the system ranges: SYSTEM-LEVEL-MAX >= PORT-LEVEL-MAX >= PORT-LEVEL-MIN >= SYSTEM-LEVEL-MIN, and the authority sets must be included in the system sets. Implementations must be able to hold at least 256 distinct authority flag fields in each set. A system that does not separate data by level should use trivial ranges where all four level values are equal.
sections.eli5: Each machine has a rule book saying the lowest and highest secrecy it may handle and which agencies' packets it accepts. Each door of the machine has a narrower rule inside that.

sections.title: Processing and Error Handling
sections.content:
On input, a received option is checked in three steps: the level must be a valid, non-reserved value; PORT-LEVEL-MAX must be at least the datagram's level; and the datagram's authority flags must be included in PORT-AUTHORITY-IN. If the port requires the option and it is missing, that is an error. On output, no datagram may be sent with a label outside the port's configured range.

Systems that handle classified data must generally label outgoing datagrams. The exception is dedicated or system-high networks, where traffic may be labelled implicitly by the port it arrives on. Where both labelled and unlabelled traffic are allowed, the RFC recommends sending unlabelled by default. If the destination demands labels it answers with an ICMP error, and the sender then labels later packets to it, which needs a per-destination cache.

Datagrams with errors should not be delivered to user processes. A missing required option gets ICMP Parameter Problem Missing Option (type 12, code 1), with the pointer set to 130. A malformed option gets Parameter Problem (type 12, code 0). An out-of-range datagram gets Destination Unreachable, Communication Administratively Prohibited (type 3, code 9 for net or code 10 for host). Responses carry a Basic option with level PORT-LEVEL-MIN and flags PORT-AUTHORITY-ERROR. No response is sent to an ICMP message that triggers an error.
sections.eli5: When a packet arrives, the machine checks the sticker against its rule book. If the sticker is missing, odd or too secret for that door, the packet is turned away with a note saying why.

sections.title: The Extended Security Option
sections.content:
The Extended option (type 133) carries labelling information beyond the Basic option. It must be copied on fragmentation, can appear more than once if the header has room, and may appear only together with a Basic option. Its minimum length is 3 octets.

An Additional Security Info Format Code (one octet) says how to read the following information. For each code an RFC is to be published giving the syntax and an algorithm for accepting or rejecting a datagram, and the IANA assigns the code. Activities are to submit plans to DISA DISDB for review and approval. A datagram is in error if the Extended option has no Basic option, if the length is inconsistent, if the code is not registered, or if the data does not match the defining RFC.
sections.eli5: The extended sticker is a blank card with a code on it. The code tells you which instruction sheet to use to read the rest.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC notes that correct implementation of the software and hardware that process these options is essential, and that confidence in it is outside its scope. The options include no protection for the integrity of labels in transit, other than the IP checksum, so extra technology is needed whenever datagrams cross hostile communication environments.

Careful, secure management of each system's configuration variables is also essential for the options to give the intended security.
sections.eli5: A sticker can be tampered with on the way, so the packets need extra protection in unsafe places, and the rule books must be guarded.

items.label: Field Termination Indicator
items.desc: 0 on the final octet, 1 if more follow.

references.text: Department of Defense Directive 5200.28, "Security Requirements for Automated Information Systems," 21 March 1988.
